newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Radical Basque youth wage street violence.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Radical Basque youth wage street violence.

text.p: Behind a door scarred by police explosives, glassy-eyed Basque youths in a dark, dank flat faithfully recite the rhetoric of the separatist guerrilla group ETA to justify their weekly rampages of vandalism.

Activists of the radical youth group Jarrai ("Go Forward" in the Basque language Euskera), describe their frequent attacks on buses, banks and businesses as spontaneous expressions of fury at repression by the Spanish state.
Basque officials say the street violence is a campaign carefully orchestrated by ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).
"Jarrai sees the fight in the streets as legitimate," said David Zelaia, a 21-year-old activist with long, dishevelled hair and tobacco-stained teeth.
"We don't have any reservations about saying we support this type of struggle against Spanish interests and against people who are trafficking in the suffering of others, like the banks."

Zelaia was speaking at Jarrai's headquarters in the old quarter of Bilbao, the commercial centre of the Basque region of northern Spain. The front door of the stale-smelling apartment bears the marks of explosives used during a police raid.
Like ETA, Jarrai wants an independent Basque state. But unlike the guerrilla group which has killed some 800 people in the past 29 years, Jarrai's main weapon is "Kale Borroka", or street violence.
